column1: # rule<TAB>why it matters (printed under each gate row). One line per rule; add a line when you add a rule.

column2: no k6 data means nothing was measured; every other PASS would be meaningless
a cutover without traffic proves nothing: every other rule would pass on silence (k6 must not stop or stall around the switch)
relying parties pin the issuer; a token whose iss differs from its network's issuer is rejected (or worse, accepted from a forged host)
any 5xx or dropped connection during the deployment is downtime that a user or an app actually sees
resource servers fetch discovery + JWKS to validate tokens; if these fail, every API call in the estate starts failing
apps authorize on sub/iss and our custom claims (tenant, login_ctx); a token missing them breaks authorization downstream
sub is the user's identity in every downstream app; a changed sub looks like a different person (lost data, duplicate accounts)
a user mid-login during the flip (started on the old version, finishing on the new) must not be thrown out of the login
sessions created before the switch must keep refreshing afterwards, or every logged-in user is logged out by a deployment
invalid_grant on refresh = a session the server forgot; for a shared-DB switch nothing may be forgotten
a session the user logged out of must stay dead; if it refreshes again, a logout did not protect the user (security)
lossy overlap: only sessions created inside the copy window may be lost; anything else lost is real data loss
sessions older than the copy point exist on both databases; losing one of them means the copy or migration lost data
a lost session must be recoverable silently via the legacy IdP's SSO; if the re-login fails, the user is really locked out
logouts done on the old version during the window are replayed; if replay misses one, that session comes back to life (security)
the same in-flight guarantee for the flip back: a rollback must not break users who are mid-login
sessions from before the switch must survive a rollback too; a rollback must not log everybody out
users who logged in on the NEW version must stay logged in after the rollback, or a rollback logs out everyone who arrived after the switch
lossy rollback: sessions may only be lost where the design says (window on the way out, green-only sessions on the way back)
sessions older than the copy point must still work after rolling back to the old database
logouts done on the new version are reverse-replayed onto the old one; a miss resurrects that session after the rollback (security)
users created on the new version must keep their sub when we roll back, or they come back as a different identity
how long a rollback takes from decision to flip: the time users are exposed to a bad release after we notice
length of the window in which new sessions on the old version will be lost: the blast radius of a lossy upgrade
how many users had to re-login because of the upgrade (silent via SSO here; visible if the IdP session had expired)
how many silent re-logins the lost sessions caused: extra load on Keycloak and the legacy IdP right after the cutover
logouts carried over from the old version; each one would otherwise be a resurrected session
users first created on the old version during the window; each one would otherwise get a new sub on the new version
time during which a logout made on the old version could still be undone on the new one: the security exposure window
sessions created on the new version that a lossy rollback throws away (users re-login once)
silent re-logins caused by the rollback
logouts from the new version carried back onto the old one by the rollback
users created on the new version, recreated on the old one with the same id by the rollback
exposure window after a rollback during which a logout made on the new version could still be undone
sessions from the forward window that work again after rolling back to the old DB (they were never really gone there)
a real app's login (app -> Keycloak -> legacy IdP -> app) must end with an app session; a failure is a user who clicked "log in" and is not logged in
resource servers that introspect ask Keycloak on every request; an introspection error or a false "inactive" rejects a logged-in user's API call (a 401 in the middle of their work)
resource servers validate JWTs locally against Keycloak's keys and issuer; a rejected JWT from a live session means every API call of that user fails
apps refresh tokens through their OAuth2 library and do NOT re-login on their own; a lost refresh means the user is thrown out of the app at the next token expiry

apps learn about a Keycloak logout only through the back-channel call; if it is missing or the app does not act on it (a logout at Keycloak or in another app), the app session outlives the logout (the user thinks they logged out but the app still lets them in: security)
slow back-channel delivery widens the time in which an app still serves a session that Keycloak already ended
front-channel apps are logged out by the browser loading their logout URL from Keycloak's logout page; if the URL is missing or does nothing, the app session survives the logout (security)
after a user logs out of an app, nothing may keep working with that session; a successful call after logout is a logout that did not protect the user (security)
login hop latency before / during / after the cutover: how much slower logging in feels while we deploy
code-exchange latency before / during / after the cutover: the last step of every login
token refresh latency before / during / after the cutover: every logged-in client pays it in the background
end-to-end latency of an app's API call with a locally validated JWT (includes the app's token refresh): what users of the app feel
end-to-end latency of an app's API call validated by introspection: every such call waits on Keycloak, so a slow Keycloak slows the app
Keycloak's introspection latency as the resource server sees it: the direct cost of the cutover on every introspecting API
step classes whose p95 during the cutover is more than twice their pre-switch p95: where users feel the deployment even without errors
proves the lossy window really happened: a session made on the old version after the copy is unknown to the new one (else the lossy rules passed on no data, or the new DB saw writes it should not)
